faqs.question: What is the main difference between garba and dandiya?
faqs.answer: Garba is danced in a circle with hand claps around a lamp or an image of the goddess, and needs no partner or props. Dandiya raas is danced with two sticks that you strike against a partner's, and Gujarati tradition links it with Krishna's raas.

faqs.question: Is garba and dandiya same or different?
faqs.answer: They are different dances that share the same Navratri nights. Event posters often say "raas garba" because both are played in one evening, usually garba first and dandiya later.

faqs.question: Do you need a partner to play garba?
faqs.answer: No. Garba is a circle, so you join the ring and follow the person ahead of you. Dandiya raas is the one that needs a partner, because your sticks strike those of the dancer beside or opposite you.

faqs.question: Which is easier for a beginner, garba or dandiya?
faqs.answer: Garba, in our practical observation, because you only copy the step and claps of the person ahead. In dandiya a missed count can bring your stick down on a partner's hand, so start in a slower outer line.

faqs.question: What is the difference between garba and garbi?
faqs.answer: A garbo is the pierced clay pot with a lamp inside, while a garbi, in some parts of Gujarat, is a wooden stand holding several lamps that men sometimes lift onto their heads while dancing. Garbi is also a short song form, though the art historian Jyotindra Jain says the line between garbo and garbi songs does not hold up in actual poems.

faqs.question: Is raas the same as dandiya raas?
faqs.answer: No. Raas is a family of circle dances; a 12th-century text names three forms, and the stick form, dandarasaka, is what we now call dandiya raas. Some raas forms in Gujarat are still danced without sticks.

faqs.question: Do dandiya sticks represent Durga's swords?
faqs.answer: That is a popular reading, not a documented origin. A 16th-century description quoted by Jyotindra Jain treats them as thumb-thick wooden sticks wrapped in silk, with no mention of swords.

faqs.question: Can men dance garba?
faqs.answer: Yes, at almost every Navratri event today. Garba was historically danced mainly by women, while the organised raas troupes of Saurashtra were all-male.

faqs.question: What should I wear for garba and dandiya?
faqs.answer: The same outfit works for both: chaniya choli for women and a kediyu for men at most events. Traditional raas troupes wear kediyu, choyani trousers, a paghadi turban and a bhet cloth tied at the waist.

faqs.question: When does Navratri start in 2027?
faqs.answer: Sharad Navratri 2027 begins on Thursday 30 September, with Maha Navami on Friday 8 October, per Drik Panchang for New Delhi. Garba and dandiya are played on each of the nine nights.

faqs.question: Can I ask someone to be my garba buddy instead of a dandiya partner?
faqs.answer: Yes. The Be My Dandiya Partner page has a garba buddy version that asks "Will you be my garba buddy, all nine nights?" It is meant for one person, not a group.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Garba vs Dandiya Difference: Claps in a Circle, Sticks in Pairs

**The garba vs dandiya difference in one line: garba is a circle dance kept in time by hand claps around a lamp for the goddess, while dandiya raas is a stick dance in which you strike a pair of sticks against a partner's.** Garba needs no partner and nothing in your hands. Dandiya needs both, which is why "dandiya partner" is a real dance term and "garba partner" is mostly slang.

If you want to ask one person to be your dandiya partner, timing matters: on SubhSandesh, 48.3% of shared pages are opened on a phone, and in our nearest festival measurement (Raksha Bandhan, not Navratri, n=89) 49.4% of pages were built on the festival day itself. Below are 11 points compared, each with its basis, then the garbo and garbi terms, raas versus dandiya raas, regional practice and six misconceptions.

## What is garba, and what is dandiya raas?

Garba is a devotional circle dance from Gujarat in which dancers move around a central lamp and keep the tala by clapping. Dandiya raas is one form of raas, a family of circle dances linked to Krishna, in which each dancer holds two sticks called dandiya and strikes them to keep the beat.

The art historian Jyotindra Jain, in his essay [Rasa and Garba in the Arts of Gujarat](https://www.sahapedia.org/sites/default/files/Rasa%20and%20Garba%20in%20the%20Arts%20of%20Gujarat.pdf), states the split plainly: rasa is "more connected with the cult of Krishna and garba with that of the Goddess". He also quotes Gujarati lines in which Krishna "performs garba" and the goddess Bhavani dances rasa.

Both fill the same nine nights, which is why people treat them as one. Sharad Navratri ran from 11 October in 2026 and begins on 30 September in 2027, ending with Maha Navami on 8 October ([Drik Panchang, New Delhi](https://www.drikpanchang.com/navratri/ashwin-shardiya-navratri-dates.html?year=2027&geoname-id=1261481)).

## Garba vs dandiya raas: the five differences that decide it

The table holds the five points that separate the dances. Each carries its basis: Jain's essay, folk-dance scholar Utpala Desai's [Raas Traditions of Gujarat](https://www.sahapedia.org/raas-traditions-of-gujarat) on Sahapedia, or our practical observation where no source exists.

| Point | Garba | Dandiya raas | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| Props | Nothing in the hands; a garbo pot or garbi lamp-stand at the centre | Two sticks; one 16th-century text asks for thumb-thick, sixteen-finger-long, silk-wrapped sticks | Jain |
| Partners | None; you dance with the circle | Yes; you strike sticks with a dancer beside or opposite | Desai; practical observation |
| Keeping the beat | Hand claps keep the tala | Sticks keep the tala; Maher raas uses an 11-matra tal called maniaro | Jain, Desai |
| Songs and deity | Garbo and garbi songs to the goddess | Raas geet, often on Krishna; harmonium, dhol, tabla, pavo, zanz, shehnai | Jain, Desai |
| Who traditionally danced | Mainly women | Organised troupes all-male, 16 to 20 dancers and musicians | Jain, Desai |

Six softer points follow. Most rest partly on what we have seen at events:

- **Formation:** garba moves in one or more circles round a centre (Jain). Saurashtra raas troupes dance in a circle too (Desai), but most city dandiya uses facing lines (practical observation).
- **Tempo:** raas runs from a metre-less doha to double-speed chalati, the song and a fast finale (Desai). Garba also rises within a song (practical observation).
- **Time of night:** garba usually comes first, after the aarti, and dandiya later (practical observation).
- **Dress:** raas troupes wear kediyu, choyani, paghadi turban and bhet waist cloth (Desai). At garba, chaniya choli and kediyu are the norm (practical observation).
- **Beginner difficulty:** garba is easier because you copy the person ahead; in dandiya a missed count can hit a hand (practical observation).
- **Where and when:** garba is danced at Navratri and after weddings at the Adalaj stepwell (Jain); raas also fills Janmashtami fairs and Saurashtra weddings (Desai).

The takeaway: the honest differences are props, partners and lineage. Tempo and time of night are habits of modern events, not rules.

## Garbo, garbi and garba: three words people mix up

A garbo is the pot. Jain describes it as "an earthen pot, its surface pierced by several holes, and with a wick-lamp inside", placed in the middle while women dance round it singing garbo songs, and the pot gave its name to both the songs and the dance.

A garbi is a different object. In some areas of Gujarat it is a wooden structure with shelves for several earthen lamps, and Jain records that when "excited by the rhythm of the dance or possessed by the goddess", a few men lift the garbi onto their heads and keep dancing.

Garbi is also a song form, supposedly compact where garbo songs are long and narrative, though Jain says the distinction "does not hold good" in actual poems. The popular derivation from Sanskrit garbha-deepa, a lamp in the womb of a pot, he calls "only conjectures", and he thinks the word more likely began in local usage.

## Raas vs dandiya raas: the stick dance is one kind of raas

Raas is the larger category, and dandiya raas is one member of it. Jain cites the 12th-century Bhavaprakashana of Sharadatanaya, which names three forms: latarasaka, dandarasaka and mandalarasaka, and he identifies dandarasaka as dandiya raas.

Raas without sticks still exists. Jain writes that "some rasa-s are performed without sticks", and art from Gujarat shows a one-stick version, partners clapping a single stick each, that he says is no longer seen in practice.

Desai lists six community raas traditions across Saurashtra and Kutch, including Kanabi, Maher, Padhar and Mishra (Gop) raas. Maher dancers use parona, thick bamboo sticks, and the Kanabis of Latipur keep a talwar (sword) raas commemorating the battle of Bhuchar Mori on 18 July 1591. That is why posters say "raas garba": the night holds both forms, not one combined dance.

## How the difference plays out in Gujarat, Mumbai and the diaspora

In Gujarat the line is blurring. Desai says one "rarely comes across the pure form of raas", because at Navratri hundreds of men and women dance it "for pure entertainment which follows no choreographic patterns", while organised mandalis in Saurashtra keep the old choreography; the Chhaya Maher Raas Mandali dates from 1967.

Desai also dates raas's spread through the rest of the state to after Saurashtra became part of Gujarat in 1960. Garba runs the other way: Jain calls it "peculiar only to Gujarat", with no mention in literature outside it.

In Mumbai, by our practical observation, "dandiya" often names the whole night, even when most of it is garba. Facing lines of stick pairs are the norm there, not the circular Saurashtra troupe form.

In the United States the two have merged on stage. Jessica Falcone's 2013 study in the [Journal of Asian American Studies](https://muse.jhu.edu/article/501357) (abstract read) describes garba-raas rebuilt as an intercollegiate competitive dance by dancers most of whom never lived in the rural Gujarat they portray, a "nostalgia without memory".

## Six misconceptions about garba and dandiya

Several of these are stated as fact on pages that rank for this question today. Each heading is the claim; the text is what the sources say.

### 1. "Garba and dandiya are the same dance"

They share a festival, not a form. Jain treats them as "two interrelated" but separate forms, each with its own songs and its own place in Gujarati poetry from the 15th century on.

### 2. "The sticks are Durga's swords"

This is a popular reading, not a documented origin. Even [Wiktionary's entry for dandiya](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/dandiya) defines it as a stick "representing a sword", dated from the 20th century. The 16th-century specification Jain quotes treats the sticks purely as wooden props wrapped in silk, and the one raas that really uses swords commemorates a 1591 battle.

### 3. "Garba is slow and dandiya is fast"

Both speed up. Desai says raas "begins on a slow pace and gradually develops into a fast rhythm", and by practical observation garba songs accelerate the same way.

### 4. "Dandiya is a couples' dance"

The person opposite you is a partner for a count, not a date. Desai writes that traditionally raas "is performed only by males", and Jain shows dandiya-rasa depicted with all women, all men, or both together. The romantic sense of "dandiya partner" is modern slang.

### 5. "Garba is only danced at Navratri"

Navratri is the main season, not the only one. Jain records villagers at the Adalaj stepwell near Ahmedabad performing garba after a marriage rite in front of a carving, dated 1499, of nine garba pots that stand for the nine forms of Durga.

### 6. "Garba comes from garbha, the womb"

It might, but nobody has shown it. Jain calls the garbha-deepa derivations conjectures and leans towards a local origin.

## Dandiya needs a partner, garba does not: asking one person

Because dandiya raas pairs you with someone, the question "will you be my dandiya partner?" has a real answer. With 48.3% of shared pages opened on a phone, an invitation sent as a link has to work on a small screen, and 90.9% of pages started on SubhSandesh are published and shared.

[Be My Dandiya Partner](https://subhsandesh.in/dandiya-partner) is built for that one person. You add nine short lines, one per night, up to six photos and the night's date, venue and dress code; they clash a pair of sticks to open it, play a short dhol-beat dandiya game, pick the colour they will twirl in, and the No button turns into a second Yes after five tries. A yes ends in a 1080×1920 Dandiya Pass, sized for an Instagram Story, and it opens without an app or an account.

If the person you have in mind is a garba friend rather than a stick partner, the same page asks "Will you be my garba buddy, all nine nights?" If the plan is a dinner after the last night rather than the dance itself, [The Invitation](https://subhsandesh.in/date-invitation) suits better, because a yes there turns into a countdown to the day.

The limits are real. The page is English-only, it is a one-to-one invitation and the wrong tool for a society, office or group invite, it does not sell garba passes or find you a partner, and it will not teach either dance. For steps, a friend in the circle beats any page.

## Sources

- Jyotindra Jain, "Rasa and Garba in the Arts of Gujarat", Sahapedia PDF (undated; cites works to 1981).
- Utpala Desai, "Raas Traditions of Gujarat", Sahapedia (undated, c. 2015).
- Jessica Marie Falcone, "Garba With Attitude", Journal of Asian American Studies 16(1), February 2013 (abstract only).
- Wiktionary, "dandiya" (undated).
